query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin chromium coating applied to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by forming a continuous, chromium-rich protective barrier during in situ thermal activation.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that currently show limited resistance to the corrosive effects of molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin chromium coating using a surface treatment technique such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) followed by thermal activation under plating-relevant conditions.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures near 660–700°C during hot-dip processes; the chromium layer must undergo thermal activation within these temperature bounds to form the stable protective phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous chromium-rich intermetallic or oxide barrier layer at the interface between the chromium coating and boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: During the high-temperature exposure, the chromium coating diffuses and reacts to form a stable barrier that limits the diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate, thereby reducing interfacial degradation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline, uncoated boride components, the chromium-coated samples are expected to show significantly reduced corrosion depth and lower corrosion current density – potentially achieving an improvement in corrosion metrics by at least 30–50%.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without the chromium surface treatment.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the chromium coating is expected to hold under standard hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (660–700°C and typical exposure durations). Deviations such as substantially higher temperatures or prolonged exposure durations might destabilize the protective layer, reducing its effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement and the optimal coating thickness/thermal activation parameters are not yet fully defined and will require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based component samples. One set remains untreated (baseline) and the other is processed using a thin chromium coating via PVD followed by a controlled thermal activation step. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under identical conditions (660–700°C for the same duration). After exposure, compare the samples using cross-sectional imaging for corrosion depth analysis, potentiodynamic polarization tests for corrosion current density, and microstructural assessments via SEM and XRD.
measurements: Corrosion current density (Icorr, determined by electrochemical testing)
Microstructural integrity and phase analysis (SEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the chromium-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (i.e., less than a 30–50% reduction in corrosion depth and/or corrosion current density) compared to the untreated baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

occupying_moves.technique: controlled alloy synthesis followed by hot‐dip plating corrosion tests (with compositional analysis)
occupying_moves.conditions: molt aluminum exposure at typical plating temperatures (~700–750 °C) compared with a baseline non‐modified boride composition

chosen.lever: addition of a minor alloying element (e.g., titanium)
chosen.technique: controlled alloy fabrication and subsequent corrosion testing in a molten-aluminum hot-dip environment
chosen.conditions: exposure to molten aluminum at standard plating temperatures (~700–750 °C) for prescribed durations, with side-by-side comparison to the unmodified alloy
chosen.why: This intervention directly targets the open question by modifying the boride-based component’s composition to induce the formation of a protective interfacial phase—potentially a Ti-enriched boride or aluminide—that resists molten-aluminum attack. This approach, supported by prior findings on alloying benefits for high-temperature corrosion resistance, is well within standard experimental protocols in materials science.

frame.system: Boride-based components currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that, in their initial state, exhibit limited resistance to the corrosive attack by molten aluminum.
frame.goal: Improve the resistance of these components to molten-aluminum corrosion, achieving a measurable performance enhancement relative to the unmodified (baseline) boride surfaces.
frame.limitation: The current boride-based materials suffer from insufficient corrosion resistance when in contact with molten aluminum, leading to premature degradation during service.
constraints: The intervention must be a single, standalone process or modification
It must be applicable to the existing boride-based system
It should remain effective under the harsh conditions of molten aluminum exposure
frame.regime: Exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures near or above aluminum’s melting point (approximately 660–700°C) during hot-dip plating operations, under prolonged high thermal and chemical stress.
prior_attempts: Baseline components without any additional surface modification have been found to corrode too rapidly
More complex multistep treatments or alloying methods have been considered in the past but were not feasible as a single intervention solution
frame.understanding: Hypothesis: Applying a thin, refractory-metal coating—specifically a chromium layer—on the surface of boride-based components will improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance. The mechanism is proposed to involve the formation of a stable, continuous chromium-rich protective film (or intermetallic barrier) during exposure to molten aluminum. This film limits the diffusion of aluminum into the substrate, reducing interfacial degradation. The prediction is that, compared to untreated boride components, the chromium-coated components will show a significant extension in service lifetime and reduced corrosion depth (for example, an improvement by at least 30–50% in corrosion metrics). The coating should remain effective provided that the hot-dip process does not exceed the conditions under which the chromium layer forms the stable protective phase (e.g., maintained melt temperature and exposure duration). Prior evidence from high-temperature corrosion studies on similar refractory coatings supports that chromium can form a durable barrier in aggressive environments. A controlled experiment comparing identical boride component samples—with and without the chromium coating—in a molten-aluminum bath (monitoring corrosion rate, interfacial microstructures, and performance over time) would provide data that could falsify the hypothesis if no significant difference in corrosion resistance is observed.

decision.trend: Earlier studies first attempted to overcome corrosion issues by altering the bulk alloy compositions and processing conditions (including high‐entropy alloy design and plasma treatments) so as to form protective surface layers in aggressive environments. Later, researchers shifted focus to single‐step surface treatments – such as plasma jet oxidation or powder-pack boriding – that change the outer layer’s composition and microstructure, creating a barrier to corrosive attack. In both cases, the emphasis was on modifying the surface without overhauling the entire system. However, despite these advances, no streamlined, single-intervention process has yet been shown to reliably form a stable, low-diffusivity interface on existing boride substrates under molten aluminum conditions.
decision.unsolved: A simple, standalone intervention that, when applied to the existing boride-based components, creates a continuously protective and stable interfacial barrier against molten aluminum corrosion remains missing. Specifically, how to induce an adherent, chromium-enriched intermetallic or oxide layer that limits aluminum penetration without needing multistep or bulk alloy modifications is still unsolved.
decision.lever: thin chromium coating deposition via a surface treatment technique (e.g., physical vapor deposition) with subsequent in situ thermal activation
decision.why: The evolving trend shows that researchers have moved from complex alloying strategies toward targeted, single-step surface modifications that form protective films. Prior studies indicate chromium’s ability to generate durable, high-temperature resistant barriers. Thus, applying a controlled thin Cr coating on boride-based components, and thermally activating it (at plating-relevant temperatures) to form a continuous chromium-rich intermetallic/oxide layer, is the most plausible next step to improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance while meeting the niche requirement for a single intervention.
